item.title: Bhikkhus, just as a dirty, stained cloth, if a dyer dips it in this or that dye — blue, yellow, red, or magenta — it…
item.description:
Bhikkhus, just as a dirty, stained cloth, if a dyer dips it in this or that dye — blue, yellow, red, or magenta — it will take the dye poorly, it will be impure in color. Why is that? Because the cloth was not clean. So too, bhikkhus, a bad destination awaits a defiled mind. Bhikkhus, just as a clean, pure cloth, if a dyer dips it in this or that dye — blue, yellow, red, or magenta — it will take the dye well, it will be pure in color. Why is that? Because the cloth is clean. So too, bhikkhus, a good destination awaits an undefiled mind.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthasutta

item.title: How, householder, is there vain hope? Here, householder, a person thinks: 'May I have such form in the future! May I have such feeling in…
item.description:
How, householder, is there vain hope? Here, householder, a person thinks: 'May I have such form in the future! May I have such feeling in the future! May I have such perception in the future! May I have such formations in the future! May I have such consciousness in the future!' Thus, householder, is vain hope.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.3

item.title: One restrained by conscience, Who can be found in the world? Who knows how to check criticism, Like a fine horse the whip? One restrained…
item.description:
One restrained by conscience,
Who can be found in the world?
Who knows how to check criticism,
Like a fine horse the whip?
One restrained by conscience,
Always mindful,
That one attains the result,
Suffering is destroyed,
Walking with even steps
On the uneven path.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.18

item.title: Bhikkhus, when a child grows up and his faculties mature, he enjoys the full range of the five strands of sensual pleasure — forms cognizable…
item.description:
Bhikkhus, when a child grows up and his faculties mature, he enjoys the full range of the five strands of sensual pleasure — forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, stimulating sensual desire, enticing; sounds... odors... flavors... tangibles... When he sees a form with the eye, he lusts after a pleasant form and dislikes a disagreeable form; he dwells without mindfulness of the body, with a limited mind. He does not truly understand the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, where those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. Thus, for him, with regard to bodily contact, whatever feeling arises — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — he rejoices in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it. Because he rejoices, welcomes, and is attached to that feeling, delight arises. Having delight in those feelings, he is attached. With attachment as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus is the origination of this whole mass of suffering.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 38 – Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasutta

item.title: Elder Nisabha: Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, Those truly delightful things that please the mind, With faith, I went forth to make…
item.description:
Elder Nisabha:

Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,
Those truly delightful things that please the mind,
With faith, I went forth to make an end of suffering.

I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life.
I await the time, mindful and clearly comprehending.

From: Theragāthā 2.38

item.title: What do you think, Ambattha? Have you heard the brahmins who are elders, senior, teachers, and ancestors say? In the past, those ascetics among the…
item.description:
What do you think, Ambattha? Have you heard the brahmins who are elders, senior, teachers, and ancestors say? In the past, those ascetics among the brahmins, the authors of the mantras, the reciters of the mantras who sang, spoke, and compiled the sacred verses that today's brahmins sing, speak, and recite just as the former ones did. Those ascetics named Atthaka, Vāmaka, ..., Kassapa, Bhagu. Did they bathe well, groom well, keep their hair and beard well-trimmed, adorn themselves with garlands and jewels, wear white clothes, enjoy and indulge in the five strands of sensual pleasure, as you and your teacher do now?

From: Dīgha Nikāya 3 – Ambaṭṭhasutta

item.title: There are these five ways of removing resentment, bhikkhus, by which any resentment that arises in a bhikkhu should be fully removed. What five? Toward…
item.description:
There are these five ways of removing resentment, bhikkhus, by which any resentment that arises in a bhikkhu should be fully removed. What five? Toward whomever resentment arises, loving-kindness should be developed toward that person. Thus resentment toward that person should be removed. Toward whomever resentment arises, compassion should be developed toward that person. Thus resentment toward that person should be removed. Toward whomever resentment arises, equanimity should be developed toward that person. Thus resentment toward that person should be removed. Toward whomever resentment arises, non-attention and non-reflection should be practiced regarding that person. Thus resentment toward that person should be removed. Toward whomever resentment arises, the fact of one's own kamma should be established: 'The venerable one is the owner of his kamma, heir to his kamma, born of his kamma, related to his kamma, supported by his kamma. Whatever kamma he does, whether good or evil, he will be the heir of that kamma.' Thus resentment toward that person should be removed. These, bhikkhus, are the five ways of removing resentment by which any resentment that arises in a bhikkhu should be fully removed.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.161

item.title: Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: Living this life is not without its rules, But food does not come close to the heart. Because there is food, the…
item.description:
Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja:

Living this life is not without its rules,
But food does not come close to the heart.
Because there is food, the body survives.
Seeing this, I wander seeking food.

The wise have experienced that it is truly a mire.
Homage and offerings come from families.
Like a subtle arrow, hard to draw out,
So for a fool, honor is hard to abandon.

From: Theragāthā 2.2

item.title: Elder Nun Somā: That state hard to attain, Only sages attain it. With two-finger wisdom, a woman — How could she hope to attain it?…
item.description:
Elder Nun Somā:

That state hard to attain,
Only sages attain it.
With two-finger wisdom, a woman —
How could she hope to attain it?

What does womanhood matter
When the mind is well concentrated,
When wisdom unfolds,
Rightly seeing the sublime Dhamma?

Everywhere, delight is destroyed,
The mass of delusion is shattered.
Know thus, Evil One!
You are Death, you are defeated.

From: Therīgāthā 3.8
